analysis.one_liner: Strengthens equal-pay enforcement for women, bans salary-history screening, and requires large employers to report pay data.
analysis.headline: The bill won approval from the Senate labor committee and had 52 senators behind it, but sat on the Senate calendar for 17 months and never got a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten federal law against paying women less than men for the same work. It would make it much harder for employers to justify a pay gap, add compensatory and punitive damages and class-action tools for workers, bar employers from firing people who share their wages, and forbid employers from using a job applicant's past salary to set a lower offer. It would also require large employers to report pay broken down by sex, race, and ethnicity so regulators can spot patterns.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — especially women, and women of color, who the bill's findings say still earn significantly less than men for equal work — would get stronger tools to challenge pay discrimination: harder employer defenses, compensatory and punitive damages, class actions with expert fees paid, protection from retaliation for discussing or disclosing wages, and a ban on salary-history screening that carries forward past underpayment into new job offers. Job applicants and workers at firms with 100 or more employees would also benefit from the required pay-data reporting, which gives regulators evidence to target investigations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, especially women facing pay discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Narrows the employer's legal escape hatch: a pay gap could only be justified by a bona fide factor such as education, training, or experience that is job-related, consistent with business necessity, and accounts for the entire differential — and not at all if a cheaper alternative practice exists

Adds compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, plus class-action treatment and reimbursement of expert fees, so workers can realistically afford to sue
Makes it unlawful to retaliate against workers who ask about, discuss, or disclose wages, and bans requiring employees to sign contracts or waivers barring them from disclosing pay

Bars employers from seeking or relying on a prospective employee's wage history — which carries forward past discrimination from job to job — with civil penalties of $5,000 for a first offense rising to $10,000, plus damages of up to $10,000 per affected person

Requires the EEOC to collect compensation, hiring, termination, and promotion data from employers with 100 or more employees, broken down by sex, race, and ethnicity, and publish aggregate figures by industry and area so pay gaps become visible and enforceable

Directs the Department of Labor to run a grant program for negotiation-skills training for women and girls, conduct studies on pay disparities, and publish information on wage discrimination to help the public understand and address it

analysis.who_pays: Large employers — firms with 100 or more employees — and federal contractors would bear the direct costs: new pay-data reporting, stronger investigative scrutiny from the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs, and real exposure to compensatory and punitive damages in equal-pay lawsuits. Employers would also lose the salary-history tool they currently use to calibrate offers. Compliance burdens fall mainly on employers, while the negotiation-training grants, studies, and enforcement are paid for with federal funds ("such sums as may be necessary"). Small enterprises exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act are carved out.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: employers with 100 or more workers would have to file detailed compensation, hiring, termination, and promotion data annually, and the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in federal spending with no cost cap

The damages provision could push employers toward settling even weak claims, since compensatory and punitive damages and attorney and expert fees raise the cost of defending any pay-structure challenged as not a 'business necessity'

The salary-history ban removes information some employers use to gauge market rates; the bill allows employers to consider voluntarily disclosed past pay only after making an offer, which supporters see as stopping discrimination from compounding and critics see as less accurate pricing of candidates
Coverage is limited to firms above the Fair Labor Standards Act's small-enterprise exemption, so workers at many small businesses get none of these protections

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are concrete: enforceable remedies, wage transparency, and an end to salary-history screening that locks in past underpayment. The costs — reporting paperwork for large employers, some added litigation exposure, and federal spending on training grants — are modest relative to the stakes and are blunted by the small-business exemption, a six-month phase-in, and mandatory technical-assistance materials for small enterprises. The main design question is whether the business-necessity standard will be applied sensibly or become a litigation battleground in both directions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee approved it and put it on the Senate calendar in July 2023, but Senate leaders never scheduled floor time and the bill died when Congress ended without anyone voting on it.

narrative.text: Senator Murray introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, with Senator Schumer and 49 other Democrats and independents as cosponsors, and it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
On June 21, 2023 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on July 18, 2023 Chairman Sanders reported it to the Senate
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 134) — meaning it was waiting for floor time — and that is where it stayed

No floor vote ever occurred. The bill ended the Congress with 52 senators (48 Democrats and 3 independents) signed on and no Republican support, and because a Senate filibuster requires 60 votes to cut off debate, it would have needed at least 8 Republican votes that were never in evidence
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill — like Paycheck Fairness Act versions in every recent Congress — died without a vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay differently by sex are better off: the current, weaker Equal Pay Act enforcement regime — no mandatory pay-data reporting, salary-history screening allowed, no punitive damages — remains the law, and no senator ever had to cast a record vote on it.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up 51 cosponsors

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through committee — ordered reported favorably in June 2023 and formally reported it without amendment on July 18, 2023

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; as the senator who sets the floor schedule, he never brought it up for a vote after it reached the calendar in July 2023

for.name: 51 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a majority of the Senate but far short of the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the party has consistently opposed the Paycheck Fairness Act in past Congresses; their unified opposition meant the bill could not clear a 60-vote filibuster

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed Paycheck Fairness Act versions, arguing the damages, reporting mandates, and litigation provisions impose heavy costs on employers

sides.party_line_note: All 52 senators backing the bill — 48 Democrats and 3 independents — were Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsored, and no roll-call vote ever took place to record the split on the floor.

industries.note: These firms would face mandatory pay-data reporting by sex, race, and ethnicity, harder legal defenses for pay gaps, and exposure to compensatory and punitive damages in class actions. Their interest in defeating the bill runs directly against workers seeking equal pay, since the enforcement mechanisms operate by charging these employers for discriminatory gaps.

The bill requires the contract-compliance office to use a full range of investigative tools, to survey at least half of all nonconstruction contractor establishments each year, and to act on the findings. Contractors would be audited for pay discrimination more aggressively than the current status quo.

industries.industry: HR compliance, payroll, and employment-law services
industries.note: New reporting obligations and a six-month compliance window would generate work for firms that prepare EEOC filings and defend or prosecute pay claims. Their gain is a byproduct of the bill, not its purpose.
